Eggs of Chinese gizzard shad (Clupanodon thrissa) are demersal and adhesive, with the newly fertilised ovum measuring approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams] in wet mass, a value derived from the typical egg diameter of this species which ranges from 1 to 4 millimeters. When incubated at a stable water temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], the embryonic development proceeds rapidly, culminating in chorion rupture and larval eclosion after just 5.5 days [ab = 5.5 days]. This brief incubation period is characteristic of small-bodied clupeiform fishes spawning in warm, productive coastal waters, where the rapid transition from an endotrophic yolk-sac larva to an exogenously feeding pelagic larva is critical for survival. The lekithotrophic prolarva emerges with a modest yolk reserve that sustains it through the initial hours before first exogenous feeding, a period during which the larva is highly vulnerable to starvation and predation. Such a short embryonic phase reflects an adaptive strategy to maximize larval survival in relatively warm and predictable subtropical environments.

Once the yolk-sac larva transitions to exogenous feeding, the pelagic larval phase of Chinese gizzard shad begins in earnest. This free-swimming, planktonic larva undergoes rapid somatic growth within the warm estuarine habitats it favors. Individuals reach the total length associated with the onset of puberty at 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters], a milestone that marks the beginning of gonadal recrudescence and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. The size at which this reproductive activation occurs is relatively small compared to some larger clupeids, reflecting an early maturation strategy suited to a short-lived, highly fecund life history. Field surveys indicate that most individuals attain this length within their first year of life, allowing them to participate in the spawning aggregations that occur during the warmer months.

The maximum recorded total length for this species is 26 centimeters [Li = 26 centimeters], representing the upper limit of somatic growth observed in adult populations. This ultimate length is attained gradually over the course of several years and is typically achieved only by the oldest, most successful individuals within a cohort. In contrast to the rapid early growth phase, the approach to this asymptotic length slows considerably as metabolic resources are increasingly diverted toward reproductive effort rather than continued somatic expansion. Comparative data from related species within the family Clupeidae suggest that a maximum length of 26 centimeters [Li = 26 centimeters] is near the median for coastal filter-feeding clupeiforms of similar trophic ecology, placing Chinese gizzard shad in an intermediate position with respect to body size among its ecological guild.

Under the controlled thermal conditions that typify the species' natural habitat in subtropical estuaries, which are consistently near 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C] during the spawning season, the maximum lifespan of Chinese gizzard shad has been determined to be 2,920 days [am = 2,920 days]. This longevity estimate, equivalent to approximately eight years, is derived from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age determination of the oldest documented individuals. Such a lifespan is moderately extended for a clupeid of this body size, suggesting a comparatively slow senescence rate that may be linked to the species' iteroparous reproductive strategy and the relatively stable thermal environment it occupies. Individuals nearing the end of their natural lifespan show signs of physiological deterioration and reduced condition factor, consistent with the progressive organ failure associated with reproductive senescence. The combination of stable thermal conditions and reduced predation pressure in estuarine refugia likely contributes to this prolonged survival.

The Chinese gizzard shad Clupanodon thrissa exhibits a life-history strategy that balances early size at puberty with a moderately extended reproductive window, allowing multiple spawning seasons over a period of up to eight years. At 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], the rapid incubation of just 5.5 days [ab = 5.5 days] from egg to hatching maximizes the production of 0.00032-gram prolarvae (0.00032 grams) [Wwb = 0.00032 grams] during warm months. This reproductive output, combined with an ultimate adult length of 26 centimeters [Li = 26 centimeters] and a puberty threshold of 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters], underscores a fitness trade-off between early maturation and sustained somatic growth typical of iteroparous coastal clupeiforms. Such a pattern is consistent with life-history theory predictions for species occupying productive but seasonally variable subtropical estuarine ecosystems.
